Counsellor's note, 14 August. Seema Varghese, school counsellor.
Jomon (Class 10) came to see me in July, worried about maths. He said, "I always mean to study after dinner, but I pick up my phone first and then it's eleven." We talked about planning a trigger instead of relying on willpower. He wrote his own rule on a card: "If I've finished dinner, then the maths book comes out before I touch my phone." He stuck it on his cupboard. Today he showed me his tracker: on twenty-three of the last thirty evenings, he opened the book first. He said the hardest part is the first two minutes, and after that he usually keeps going. His last unit test went from 18 to 29 out of 40. What I did next: I asked if he'd like to add a second rule for Sunday mornings. He's thinking about it.

qa.q: What rule did Jomon write on the card?
qa.a: "If I've finished dinner, then the maths book comes out before I touch my phone."

qa.q: What does Jomon find hardest, and what does that suggest?
qa.a: The first two minutes are hardest, which suggests Jomon feels reluctant at the start, but once the cue gets him going, carrying on feels much easier.

qa.q: Why might this if-then rule work better than 'I always mean to study after dinner'?
qa.a: It ties a clear action to a clear cue, so after dinner he doesn't have to decide; he just follows the rule.

qa.q: How might Seema see Jomon's twenty-three evenings?
qa.a: Seema likely sees real progress built on his own rule, which is why Seema offers a second one rather than taking over.

grounding: A counsellor records a teenager using an after-dinner if-then rule to open his maths book before his phone.

Tuesday, 3 September
Day 6 of my new rule! I wrote it inside my maths notebook in pink: IF dinner plate is in the sink, THEN maths book opens BEFORE phone.
Tonight Harish bhaiya was watching cricket and shouting at the TV, and my phone buzzed on the sofa. Old me would have grabbed it. But I washed my plate, came straight to my desk and opened the book. I didn't even have to argue with myself; the rule had already decided. 😊
Did twelve questions on linear equations. Got nine right! Then checked the phone. It was just the class group sending stickers anyway.
Harish bhaiya saw me studying and said, "Who are you and what have you done with Parul?" Ha.
Parul

qa.a: Nine out of twelve.

qa.a: Parul felt calm and proud, because the if-then rule had already decided what comes after the plate goes in the sink, so there was no choice left to fight over.

qa.a: It was tied to a clear cue, the plate in the sink, and a clear action, opening the maths book, so it worked without in-the-moment willpower.

qa.q: What does Harish bhaiya's joke suggest about how he sees the change?
qa.a: He is surprised and amused to see Parul studying straight after dinner instead of reaching for the phone.

passage: In Rekha's house in the village near Nashik, dinner ended at eight, and after that the one phone the family shared usually ended up with her, playing cooking videos until the lamp went out. Maths exam in three weeks. So she made a rule and told her little sister Charu: "Once the plates are washed, maths first. Then phone." She wrote it on a chit and tucked it under the plate rack. The first night the phone buzzed with a cousin's message and her hand moved. Charu pointed at the chit. Rekha groaned but pulled out her book. By the second week she didn't need the chit. Plates in the rack, book out, as automatic as washing her hands. Soon Charu started doing the same with her Marathi homework.

qa.q: Where did Rekha tuck the chit?
qa.a: She tucked it under the plate rack.

qa.q: What was Rekha feeling when the cousin's message buzzed on the first night?
qa.a: She was tempted, since her hand moved toward the phone, and a little annoyed when Charu pointed at the chit, but she also wanted to keep her own rule.

qa.q: What choice on the first night set the pattern for the weeks after?
qa.a: Pulling out the book when Charu pointed at the chit; following the rule once made washed plates the cue, and by the second week it happened without a debate.

qa.q: How is Charu affected by Rekha's rule?
qa.a: Charu goes from reminder to copier, starting the same routine with her Marathi homework, picking up the habit by watching her older sister 😊

passage: In Accra, dinner at Kofi's house was jollof most Fridays, and after dinner used to mean the phone: videos, then the group chat, then midnight. Mock exams were in April. Kofi's cousin Dalia, who was at university, told him about if-then plans. So he wrote on a sticky note: IF the plates are cleared, THEN the maths book opens, phone after. He stuck it on the fridge. The first night, stacking plates, he felt the phone's weight in his pocket. He looked at the fridge, sighed, and opened to simultaneous equations. On the third night he forgot the note completely and still opened the book. "It's like brushing my teeth now," he texted Dalia later. "Weird." "Told you 😊," she replied.

qa.q: What did Kofi write on the sticky note?
qa.a: IF the plates are cleared, THEN the maths book opens, phone after.

qa.q: What does Kofi's sigh on the first night suggest?
qa.a: He still wanted the phone and felt its pull, but the note had already made the choice for him, so he went along with it, a bit reluctantly.

qa.q: What was the turning point showing the plan had taken hold?
qa.a: The third night, when Kofi forgot the note and still opened the book; clearing the plates had become the cue, so no in-the-moment decision was needed.

qa.q: How might Dalia feel reading 'It's like brushing my teeth now'?
qa.a: Dalia is probably pleased and a bit amused, glad that an idea from university actually helped her cousin through the evenings before mocks.

passage: In their house in Nagaur, evenings used to go the same way for Devika: dinner, then the phone, then suddenly it was eleven and her maths book was still in her bag. Telling herself 'I'll study tonight' never worked. So on Sunday she wrote a sentence on the inside cover of her maths notebook: If dinner is over, then I open this book before I touch my phone. Her sister Sunaina read it and laughed. 'That's it? That's your big plan?' 'It's specific,' Devika said. On Monday, after dinner, her hand went to her pocket out of habit. Then she remembered the sentence. She put her plate in the sink, took out the notebook, and opened it. Once it was open, starting was easy. By Friday it happened almost without thinking. The phone still came out, just after twenty sums instead of before.

qa.q: Where did Devika write her sentence?
qa.a: She wrote it on the inside cover of her maths notebook.

qa.q: How did Devika feel when Sunaina laughed at the plan?
qa.a: She felt calm and confident, trusting that a specific plan would work better than vague promises.

qa.q: Why did the 'if dinner is over, then open the book' plan work?
qa.a: It linked a clear cue, the end of dinner, to one action, opening the book, so she didn't have to decide in the moment.

qa.q: How might Sunaina see the plan by Friday?
qa.a: Sunaina might be surprised it worked, seeing her sister open the maths book almost automatically.

grounding: A teenager writes an if-then plan to open her maths book after dinner before touching her phone, and the cue replaces in-the-moment choice.

passage: Esther's afternoons in Berlin had a problem: she got home at four, dropped her bag, and her thumbs found the game before her coat was off. By six, her German vocabulary list was untouched. Her brother Felix suggested willpower. That didn't work. Then her teacher mentioned something called an if-then plan. Esther wrote on a sticky note by the front door: If I take my shoes off, then I do ten vocabulary words before anything else. It sounded almost too simple. On Monday she took off her shoes, saw the note, and did the ten words standing in the hallway, bag still on her shoulder. It took eight minutes. After a week, taking off her shoes and reaching for the list had become one movement. Felix noticed. 'You haven't touched your phone at four all week.' 'I have,' Esther said. 'At ten past.'

qa.q: Where did Esther put the sticky note?
qa.a: She put it by the front door.

qa.q: How did Esther feel about the if-then plan at first?
qa.a: She felt doubtful, since it sounded almost too simple, but was willing to try after willpower failed.

qa.q: What made Esther's plan effective?
qa.a: It tied a specific cue, taking her shoes off, to a small action, ten vocabulary words, so the choice didn't rest on in-the-moment willpower.

qa.q: How does Felix see the change?
qa.a: Felix notices she is no longer on her phone at four and seems surprised by the difference.

grounding: A teenager ties a specific cue, taking off her shoes, to ten vocabulary words, so the plan replaces in-the-moment choice.

passage: At the residential school in Aligarh, the study bell rang at seven every evening. For Asif, it used to be the signal to check his phone 'one last time', which usually meant forty minutes of videos. His roommate Samir had read somewhere about if-then plans and dared him to try one. Asif wrote it on the first page of his physics notebook: If the study bell rings, then I open this notebook and solve one problem before anything else. On Tuesday the bell rang. His hand moved toward his phone, and then he saw the notebook lying on top of it, where he had left it on purpose. He opened it. One problem became four. By Friday, the bell and the notebook felt connected. Samir, who hadn't made any plan, was still watching videos at 7:40. Asif grinned and threw a pencil at him.

qa.q: What time did the study bell ring?
qa.a: It rang at seven every evening.

qa.q: How did Asif feel by Friday about the study bell?
qa.a: He felt steadier and more in control, since the bell had become a cue for the notebook rather than the phone.

qa.q: Why did putting the notebook on top of the phone help the if-then plan?
qa.a: It made the planned action the first thing he saw at the cue, so the right choice became automatic rather than a struggle.

qa.q: How might Samir feel watching Asif work while he watches videos?
qa.a: Samir might feel a bit sheepish, since he suggested the idea but hadn't tried it himself.

grounding: A teenager at a boarding school uses an if-then plan tied to the study bell to open his notebook before his phone.

Subject: The plan actually worked

Dear Sarita Di,

You told me in the summer to stop saying “I'll study more” and make an if-then plan instead. I thought it sounded too simple. I was wrong.

My plan: If it's after dinner, then I open my maths book before I touch my phone. That's it. No “maybe,” no deciding.

The first week was hard. I'd finish dinner and my hand would reach for the phone. But then I'd remember the rule and open the book. After about ten days, it became automatic. I don't even think about it now.

My maths test last week: 78. Last term I got 54.

I think the trick is that I don't have to choose every night. The choice was already made.

Thank you.
Sumit

qa.q: What was Sumit's if-then plan?
qa.a: If it's after dinner, then Sumit opens the maths book before touching the phone.

qa.q: How did Sumit feel in the first week of the plan?
qa.a: Sumit felt tempted and it was hard, with a hand reaching for the phone, before the habit became automatic.

qa.q: Why did the if-then plan work for Sumit?
qa.a: A specific cue, after dinner, linked to a set action meant there was no nightly choice to make.

qa.q: How might Sarita Di feel reading this email?
qa.a: Sarita Di would likely feel happy and proud that the advice helped Sumit's marks go up.

grounding: The email shows a teenager using an if-then plan linking after dinner to opening the maths book, reducing reliance on in-the-moment choices.

Rekha, you keep asking how I got my science marks up. Okay, here's the whole secret, and it's going to sound stupid.
I'm Ishita. Every night, I used to finish dinner, pick up my phone “for five minutes,” and look up and it'd be eleven. Every night I'd promise tomorrow would be different.
Then our counsellor told us about if-then plans. Not “I'll study harder.” Something exact.
So I made mine: If I've just put my plate in the sink, then I open the science book on the table before the phone.
That's it. Plate in sink, book open.
Week one I had to repeat it in my head like a mantra. By week three I didn't even think. Plate, book. My phone sits on the shelf until I've done an hour.
My science went from a C to a B-plus. It's not magic. It's just one less decision.

qa.q: What did Ishita's if-then plan link together?
qa.a: Putting the plate in the sink and opening the science book before the phone.

qa.q: How did Ishita feel about the nightly promises before the plan?
qa.a: Ishita felt frustrated and let down each night, promising tomorrow would be different.

qa.q: Why does the specific cue work better than “I'll study harder”?
qa.a: It ties a clear action to a daily event, so Ishita doesn't need to decide in the moment.

qa.q: How might Rekha respond to hearing the “secret”?
qa.a: Rekha might feel surprised by how simple it is and curious to try a plan like it.

grounding: The monologue shows a teenager using an if-then plan tied to a specific cue after dinner, reducing reliance on in-the-moment choices.

"Jahnavi, you keep saying you'll study after one video. Your Manoj mama was the same. Let me tell you how I got out of it.
When I was fifteen, the problem was the radio cricket commentary and the comics my friend lent me. Every evening I said I'd study "soon." Soon became ten o'clock.
One day my maths teacher said, 'Stop deciding every night. Decide once.' So I wrote on a card: If dinner is over, then the maths book opens before anything else. I stuck it on the steel almirah.
The first week I grumbled. But after dinner I didn't have to argue with myself. The card had already argued. By the half-yearly exam I'd finished the whole algebra book.
It's not magic. It just means you don't have to be strong every single evening."

Saurabh's cousin's wedding filled the house in Kanpur for a whole week: relatives on every mattress, a dholak in the courtyard, and the pre-board maths exam ten days away. His phone never stopped. Family photos, dance videos, cousins tagging him.
On the first night he lost two hours to reels. On the second morning, he took a chit and wrote: If dinner is over, then maths book open, phone with Manoj bhaiya. He showed it to his older cousin Manoj. "You'll take it from me?"
"Every night," Manoj said. "Till the exam."
That evening the dholak started again, louder. After dinner, Saurabh didn't debate. He passed his phone to Manoj, took his book to the only quiet spot, the stairs to the roof, and did twelve sums while the courtyard sang below.

qa.q: Where did Saurabh study after dinner?
qa.a: He took his book to the stairs to the roof, the only quiet spot.

qa.q: Why did Saurabh write the chit on the second morning?
qa.a: He felt frustrated and worried after losing two hours to reels, and wanted a plan that would work even with the wedding noise.

qa.q: Why did the if-then chit work even with the dholak playing?
qa.a: It tied a clear cue, the end of dinner, to a clear action, handing the phone to Manoj and opening the book, so he didn't have to decide in the moment.

qa.q: How might Manoj feel being given this job during the wedding?
qa.a: Manoj might feel trusted and a bit proud to help, happy to hold the phone even while the celebrations go on.

passage:
Madhuri had stuck a yellow note on her bedroom wall in the Gachibowli flat: AFTER DINNER → MATHS BOOK FIRST, PHONE SECOND.
She was fifteen and tired of her own promises. For weeks she had said "only ten minutes" of scrolling after dinner and looked up at eleven.
Tonight, the dinner plates were barely in the sink when her phone buzzed. Her brother Yogesh waved his. "New video from that dance crew. You have to see it."
Madhuri felt the pull. Then she looked at the note. "After maths," she said.
"Since when?"
"Since this note."
She didn't have to decide anything. The decision was already on the wall. She opened the book to quadratic equations. When she finished the exercise forty minutes later, she watched the video, and it was just as good.

qa.q: What did Madhuri's yellow note say?
qa.a: It said: AFTER DINNER → MATHS BOOK FIRST, PHONE SECOND.

qa.q: What was Madhuri feeling when Yogesh waved the video at her?
qa.a: She felt the pull of temptation, but also steady, because the note on the wall meant she did not have to fight it out in the moment.

qa.q: What would you advise someone who keeps saying "only ten minutes"?
qa.a: Make a clear if-then plan like Madhuri's, tying a specific cue such as the end of dinner to one action, and write it where you will see it.

qa.q: How might Yogesh see Madhuri's new rule?
qa.a: Yogesh seems surprised and a bit puzzled, asking "Since when?" because he is used to her watching videos straight after dinner.

grounding: It shows a teenager using a written if-then plan, maths book after dinner, so she relies less on choosing in the moment.
